Messages.Author: Vincent
Messages.Body:
First of all, I find the current system fine. But for people who think
self-ousting is unacceptable, and that there should always be hope for
0.5 vp, here's an alternate rule:

Any player (under some conditions described below) may decide to
"leave" the game:
1/ All his/her cards and counters stay in play.
2/ He/she still take his/her turn but...
3/ He/she cannot perform any action, play any card, or block or cast
vote or make choices ("may" or "can"). In fact, the player is out of
the game and cannot do anything.
4/ He/she gain 1 pool at the beginning of the turn, or 2 pool if he/
she has the Edge (this is an exception to rule 3/ concerning choices,
see remarks).
5/ Any player, except his predator, may "oust" him or her as an action
directed to all the players (so any player may block).
6/ If there is only one player left, judge should decide if the
remaining player can oust the remaining prey(s), ignoring the time
limit.
7/ If there is no player in play (may happen on a vote that ousts all
the "ready" Methuselahs), players who has left the game each gain 0.5
vp. No point is awarded for the last man standing.

At the end of the game, if he or she hasn't been ousted, he or she
gains 0.5 vp

Remarks and details for each point:
1/ This allows players that were planning on stealing resources /
sending a fame vampire to torpor etc. not to have their plan spoiled
2/ Same reason: if the predator was counting on Anarch Revolt, etc. to
oust the player, or getting the Coven, the plan shouldn't be spoiled
3/ The player has decided to leave the game. Therefore he can't
interact with the other players. Mandatory effects (such as hunting
with an empty vampire, choosing a strike or taking 1 damage when in
combat with a minion with a Wolf companion) should be applied.
Optional effects should use the default (such as: my strike is a hand
strike, I may draw a card => I don't draw a card, I have chooses
either to burn 1 pool or to lose all transfers during my next
influence phase => I lose all transfers). Judge should be called in
case of disagreement. Gaining 1 from the Edge is an exception to this
rule, it becomes mandatory for that player.
4/ With no pool gain, hope to survive are very slim. 1 pool seems
reasonable, 2 pool seem too much. Gaining 2 with the Edge forces at
least the predator to move and bleed. Maybe did the leaving player
assure some kind of position with the edge. It may also be a technique
for other players (such as playing Regaining the Upper Hand ;)) to
keep that player alive.
5/ This avoids the situation where the predator could "use" his prey
to prevent his grand-prey of intercepting his damaging votes. To make
it clear: A > B > C > D > E. C has decided to "leave" the game. B
calls votes to oust D and D cannot block because he's not B's prey. D
doesn't want to spend his resources on ousting C the normal way (he
may not be able too anyway), but he may try to with a very little cost
(a cardless action that anyone can block).
6/ A "ready" player with no mean to oust his prey should not be
awarded his vp. Calling the judge avoids loosing time. The player
should be able to prove that he can oust his prey however. Being able
to bleed for 1 with 2 minions each turn should suffice.
7/ Nuf' to say

** When can a player "leave" ? **

That's a big point. I don't have an answer because it must be thought
carefully to avoid abuses. But maybe:
- if reduced to 5 pool or less
- or after half game (in time)

And the decision should be taken by a player at the end of his or her
turn.

I am in the group of people who thinks that self ousting should
somehow be prevented. If its via development changes, fine.
I think this suggestion is extremely messy though, and waaaayyy too
complex. I cant even start to imagine the amount of loopholes and
corner cases arising from this.

Personally I prefer just removing "reasonable chance" and "Life Boon"
from the usual discussions about this whenever they come up.
If you leave out the "Ahh yes, but someone could play Life Boon", then
transferring your last pool out, or killing yourself with a KRC or
paying a master card that kills you, can all be classified as not
playing to win. Transferring out leaves you 0 % chance of getting more
VPs (again, excluding Life Boon or playing for instance an anarchist
uprising that also ousts your prey). Staying in the game, in whatever
way or manor you can, should yield you a higher chance of getting a
VP.

As an example, I have once gotten a VP with no controlled minions, no
cards in my hand and only an Anarch revolt in play.
I have never gotten a VP while being at 0 pool, unless it happened by
the same effect that cost me my last pool.

I am fine with people being able to tap out completely and
transferring down to 1 pool, just to hand a VP to their predator out
of spite. At least it gives me one round where I have a chance of
doing something. Either giving them pool, rushing the predators
minions, ousting him myself, or whatever.
My real beef is with the ability to remove the last of your own pool,
in a way that doesn't give you an additional vp.

So, yeah, ban Life Boon!

> Playing Reversal of Fortunes then transferring down to 1?
> Being at 1 and handling Army of Rats before the Edge?
>

The first two require you to play specific cards from your hand.
Reversal of Fortune is a referendum, which can be blocked, voted down,
or delayed. What's more, you have to have a torpored minion in order
for Dragonbound to kill you when you have only one pool. The third
example requires your predator to have played a card (Army of Rats), a
card which all minions at the table can attempt to remove before your
untap phase.

Transferring out for the self-oust requires no cards played and cannot
be blocked or prevented by other Methusalehs, short of a specifically
timed Life Boon.

The examples you've given illustrate the point of people who are
against self-ousting: if someone can't self-oust with transfers, they
would have to play cards or rely on played cards + game state combos
in order to self-oust. These cards and game states are all things
that other players have a chance of preventing. Other players can't
prevent self-ousts through transfers.

Another player's decision to self-oust can actually cost you a game
win, but there is essentially nothing you can do to stop it.

This is a 4/5 player game and in its best from is interactive between
all players.

In the games I have been where someone has self ousted (e.g.
Ludwigshafen 2 weeks ago!) it's often either because they've played
their own game and ignored table interactions and their game has died
or because someone else on the table (prey/predator but not always)
has trumped them/thumped them/cross table shifted for 5 etc and in
someway broken the nice happy 5-player interaction model.

In the case of the player who self ousted in Ludwigshafen they'd
managed to get me down to ~4 pool but had at the same time managed to
lose every minion to hits via poor decisions to bleed (I have untapped
minion they have no stealth for instance) so once that was done they
chose to self oust.

Now i'd rather have had a turn to recoup do some safe actions that
weren't going to be blocked etc but I totally understand why the self
ousted (prey and predator had combined to remove all minions and
therefore their fun from the game) - I don't think forcing them to
stay in the game on 1 pool no minions would have been great for them
and in many ways the table should take culpability for the self oust
(me for not pointing out that if they wait for one of those shiny obf
cards I might die and her cross table buddies for not interacting with
her at all).

Basically my laboured point is that if you interact with players more
than just treating them as conquest/conquerer you'll probably get less
self ousting.

Also adding over complicated rules for something that is fairly
marginal is absurd & more importantly can be circumvented via a number
of cards that could be in play (I can only remember the evil Darby
self ousting on me in addition to the above young lady in my decade of
tournament play & again if i'd listened to him it would never have
happened - although I'm pretty sure i've killed myself on a number of

cardless action can cost you a game win may cause concern. As you
noted, transferring out is not "cardless" because you need cards in
your uncontrolled region or crypt in order to do it. The reality is
that a small minority of decks will ever run out of crypt cards.

>More generally, there are plenty of cases where "another player's

>decision to *take any one particular course of action* can actually
>cost you a game win, [and[ there is essentially nothing you can do to
>stop it."

>It's a multiplayer game. The other players are allowed to affect the
>outcome. Learn to love it, or take up a two player game.

I disagree - almost every move that another player makes can be
intercepted or mitigated by another playing who has the necessary
cards. That's not to say that you will necessarily have those cards,
but they should have the option.

As you say, it's a multiplayer game. This means that other players in
the game should be able to use resources to interfere in the actions
of other players. I think it's especially true when the action the
player takes will unequivocally give a victory point to someone at the
table.

"Like or leave it" is not a very good argument, IMO. It doesn't prove
the superiority of your position, only that the rules are currently
the way you like them.

Honestly, I'm not horribly opposed to self-ousting, although I would
definitely vote to change the rules to disallow it. I just think that
there is an inherent problem with the game when there is no guide for
sportsmanlike play at the point where a player can no longer earn more
VPs. Self-ousting seems to be done too often as a means of
retribution or kingmaking in this case.

The point is that a rule that says "you can't spend your last pool"
isn't going to stop people from effectively ousting themselves if they
want to effectively oust themselves. So if you really want a concrete
rule that prevents people from ousting themselves, it is going to take
an awful lot of work, and can easily move into making absurd rules
about how people play.

If I can't spend my last pool, can I spend down to 1 pool and tap out
my only minion? Can I play an Anarch Revolt that will kill me? Can I
not save the Famous minion in torpor that will kill me? Can I call a
Domain Challenge that will kill me? Can I choose to not play the wake
in my hand that will block the bleed that is killing me? Can I choose
to vote for the vote that will oust me?

There already is a perfectly effective rule that keeps people from
willy-nilly ousting themselves--the Play to Win rule. If you can win
the game, you must play to win the game. If you can't win the game,
you must play to maximize your VPs. If you can't reasonably expect to
win or get any more VPs, you can die in whatever manner you choose.
The vast majority of the time? You can reasonably expect to either win
or get more VPs until you are dead. So the vast majority of the time,
people can't oust themselves anyway.

In the incredibly small number of situations where you can legally
self oust, if you want to do so, you'll find a way to do so, even if
you are prohibited from spending your last pool.

> What is a "lost" position?

LSJ covered this, but I figure I'll chime in too, as you asked me :-)

A truly "lost" position, as I understand it, is hard to define, but
easy to recognize (like porn!). You look at your position. You look at
the people around you. You say "Huh. I have no reasonable chance of
getting any more VPs. I'm done.", at which point you are free to do
what you want with yourself. Luckily, any time that this is important,
there is a judge to help make the determination (i.e. in casual play,
you can do whatever you want--this discussion and topic only covers
tournament play).

There are certainly any number of situations one can invent or trump
up to prove or disprove a given position as "lost". But in general, if
the likelihood of you getting any more VPs is small enough such that
it isn't really gonna happen, you are in a "lost" position.

Keep in mind that:
-If you have a reasonable chance of surviving to the end of the game,
and getting that .5 VP, you are obligated to legally try to do so.

-If you have a reasonable chance of withdrawing to get that .5 VP, you
are obligate to attempt.

-If you have a reasonable chance of your prey dying and you getting
that VP, you are obligated to try and make that happen.

Which, in most cases, any one of these will result in someone not
being in a truly "lost" position.

> Can I act arbitrarily (going crosstable, transfering out, whatever) in pursuit
> of the 0 vp I "reasonably" have a chance at? What if my prey's first
> vamp is Uchenna who proceeds to get No Secrets when I have no stealth
> in my deck? I assume (reasonably, in my mind) that my >5% chance has
> now gone to approximately 0. Can I now transfer out?

In all of these situations, you have the not unreasonable chance of
surviving till the game times out. Which gives you .5VP. Which you are
obligated to try for.

You need to be *really* in bad shape, generally speaking, to be judged
to be in a truly lost position. Such that your ousting is imminent. As
otherwise, you will always have the reasonable chance of surviving
till the game times out, which gives you more VPs (.5) than being
ousted before that. Are you at 1 pool with no ready minions and there
are Anarch Revolts on the table and the guy with the Revolts has vote
lock? Yeah, you are probably in a truly lost position. Are you in a
crappy seat where you can't really do much, but you can wall up and
reasonably try to stay alive? Then you probably aren't in a truly lost
position.

-Peter
